Household size changes an income comparison: keep the adjusted figure beside the cash budget

Use four charts to distinguish total household income, a square-root size adjustment, a per-person amount and a separate monthly budget built from cash receipts and costs.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare income measures and build a separate monthly cash budget

Interactive planning lab

Annual income after the square-root household-size adjustment$36,000
Annual household income divided equally per person$18,000
Monthly cash remaining after only the entered budget costs$1,400

All amounts and household sizes are original hypothetical inputs, not survey observations, population averages or low-income thresholds. The first two charts illustrate Statistics Canada’s documented private-household square-root adjustment: annual household after-tax income divided by the square root of household size. The cited standard was approved 21 March 2016, modified 23 July 2026 and reviewed 25 October 2026. This comparison measure is separate from unadjusted household income and from a per-person division; it does not create or remove cash. The monthly budget is independent. Its net cash is separately entered, shared costs stay fixed and the additional cost per person is the same for every member. That cost rule is a teaching assumption, not a cost forecast derived from the equivalence scale. No taxes, benefits, survey-group assignment, age-specific needs, location costs, other expenses, intra-month payment timing, saving return or borrowing facility is calculated. Negative monthly results identify a gap in the entered cash budget, not an actual overdraft balance.

The central idea

A household-size adjustment changes the unit used for an income comparison. The household’s cash budget still needs its actual receipts, costs and number of people.

01

Identify the statistical unit and the adjustment being made

An income figure can describe an individual, a family or everyone sharing a private household. It can also be adjusted for household size. Those distinctions change what a comparison means before any personal budget is built.

Statistics Canada’s private-household standard defines adjusted after-tax income as household after-tax income divided by the square root of household size. The method recognises that people living together can share resources and that additional members need not increase costs in direct proportion to their number.

This article illustrates that documented method. The word “adjusted” can mean something else in another series, including an adjustment for prices or for public services received in kind. Read the definition attached to the particular table rather than transferring one meaning to every income statistic.

02

Calculate the three amounts without turning them into separate income streams

The default household has four people and CAD 72,000 of annual after-tax income for the statistical illustration. Its unadjusted income remains CAD 72,000.

The square root of four is two. Dividing CAD 72,000 by two gives an adjusted comparison amount of CAD 36,000. Dividing the same income by all four people instead gives CAD 18,000 per person.

These are three descriptions of one entered income amount. The household has not received CAD 72,000 plus CAD 36,000 plus CAD 18,000. The adjustment also does not mean its bank deposits fall to CAD 36,000 or that every person receives CAD 18,000.

03

Understand what the square-root scale does and leaves out

For a one-person household, both denominators equal one. At four people, the square-root adjustment divides by two while a per-person calculation divides by four. The curve shows this difference while keeping annual income fixed.

A comparison scale can represent shared resources without pricing the actual rooms, meals, transport or care a household needs. It does not record individual access to money or establish that every member benefits equally.

Households of the same size can have different costs because of ages, disability needs, location, housing and other circumstances. An identical adjusted-income amount therefore does not establish identical cash needs or a particular standard of living for two specific households.

04

Build a separate budget from independently entered monthly cash

The cash example starts with CAD 6,000 a month assumed available after deductions. This is entered separately from the annual statistical income. The tool does not automatically treat the annual amount divided by twelve as a bank-deposit forecast.

The illustrative monthly costs are CAD 2,200 shared across the household plus CAD 600 for each of four people. The per-person costs total CAD 2,400, so the remaining cash is CAD 6,000 less CAD 2,200 less CAD 2,400: CAD 1,400.

This fixed-plus-per-person cost rule is an independent teaching assumption. It is not derived from the square-root scale or presented as an observed spending estimate. The remaining amount is after only the listed costs; other expenses and saving commitments still need their own entries.

05

Change one kind of input and observe which charts should move

Increasing the annual statistical-income input changes the comparison bars and income curves. It does not create new monthly cash in the independent budget. Changing the cash-cost inputs moves the budget figures without changing the statistical adjustment.

Changing household size affects both exercises for different reasons. It changes the denominator of the income measures, while also changing the number of per-person cost amounts in the cash scenario. The tool keeps those calculations distinct.

The matrix varies household size and the additional cost per person while retaining monthly cash and shared costs. It reveals possible monthly gaps under those assumptions. It does not estimate poverty status, classify the household into an income group or measure the probability of meeting its needs.

06

Bring the comparison back to the household’s actual decisions

When reading an income headline, record its population, year, household or family unit, price basis and size adjustment. A relevant benchmark can provide context without becoming a target salary or a forecast of cash receipts.

For planning, record the money actually available, the bills due, who shares each cost and the resources accessible to each person. A fair cost-sharing rule and a workable payment calendar require more information than an equivalized income figure supplies.

The first pair of charts explains a statistical measure. The second pair shows how a deliberately simple cash model answers a different household question. Use both with their stated units and assumptions.
